prize_parts.citation: for incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, showing how trade reallocates resources across firms and shapes aggregate productivity and the gains from trade

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part B010 prize to Helpman and Melitz. The round-1 exchange did not weaken the three things I weigh most, which are a precisely identifiable core, a short credit line and a long period of testing. The core is Melitz (2003) together with Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple on exporting versus foreign direct investment. The credit line is two names, with no arbitrary cut inside the credited set. More than twenty years of firm-level evidence from many countries have tested the framework. What changed is how I would defend it and how I would write the citation. The three B010 supporters (Enflo, Strömberg and I) converge on the same point. The citation should rest on the selection and reallocation mechanism and on the gains-from-trade channel. It should not claim a welfare magnitude, and it should not claim discovery of the exporter-premia facts, since Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are uncredited. Read that way, the quantitative debate over Pareto assumptions and sufficient-statistics results concerns how large the gains are. It does not concern whether the mechanism exists. That debate is itself conducted in the framework's language, which I read as evidence of influence. I also refined my alternative B032: if the Committee prefers it, I would now support Autor, Dorn and Hanson with a citation confined to the trade-shock and local-labour-market evidence. I previously said I would lean to Autor and Hanson plus either Dorn or Katz. Hjalmarsson, Teorell and Dreber Almenberg argued that the design-based evidence is a joint Autor-Dorn-Hanson programme, and I find that persuasive. It also removes the requirement to decide the task-framework credit question first. My ranking does not rest on the count of explicit supporters, which is three for each of B014, B032 and B010. It rests on attribution cleanliness and on how well the claimed achievement is separated from its disputed magnitude.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains attribution at the edges. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum developed closely related heterogeneous-firm models and the empirical exporter facts, and none is credited on this ballot. A Helpman-Melitz prize therefore cuts through a larger lineage, and the citation can only mitigate that. The second reservation is quantitative. Welfare gains from selection depend on functional-form assumptions, and the sufficient-statistics literature suggests they may be smaller than first claimed. A prize could then be read as honouring an elegant model more than a robust quantitative finding. The third is comparative. B032 has broader opening support and design-based evidence that is easier to check against data. B032's own credit problems (Dorn versus Katz, and task-framework credit outside the list) are a different kind of problem from B010's. Finally, trade is not my field. I cannot independently confirm priority questions and I rely on common criteria and on colleagues' accounts.

responses.point: Dreber Almenberg ranks B032 first and ranks B010 below it because the quantitative welfare gains of the firm-heterogeneity model depend more on functional-form choices, such as the Pareto assumption, than transparent reduced-form designs do. She treats this as a judgement and not a decisive scientific difference.
responses.response: I accept that reduced-form designs give a more directly checkable claim, and that is the strongest argument for B032 over B010. But functional-form dependence attaches to the size of the welfare gains, and I would not make the claimed achievement depend on that size. The mechanism of selection, exporter premia and within-industry reallocation has been tested against firm-level data in many countries without relying on the Pareto assumption. A citation limited to that mechanism is not exposed to the weakness you describe. I would also say that B032's attribution is not tighter. It needs a choice between Dorn and Katz and a decision on whether the task framework is part of the achievement, and the framework's credit sits partly with Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu and Restrepo. So we differ less on science than on which uncertainty is easier to manage in a citation. Where you want persistence and inference concerns reflected in the B032 citation, I agree.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B032 first with Autor, Hanson and Dorn. She argues that the shift-share exposure design and the local labour-market evidence are a joint Autor-Dorn-Hanson contribution, and that Katz's skill-premium work is a distinct strand. She frames the citation around technology and trade shocks, with the China-shock evidence as the identified core.
responses.response: This moves my alternative. In round 1 I treated the third name as open, Dorn or Katz depending on the strand. Your argument that the design-based programme is jointly Autor-Dorn-Hanson, and that Katz's work is an earlier and separate contribution, is more convincing than my hedge. If B032 is chosen, I would support your trio with a trade-shock citation. I still have a maturity question. You and Teorell say the qualitative local-adjustment findings have held up under re-examination. As a labour economist I want to know what that rests on, namely alternative inference for shift-share designs and longer-horizon follow-up of exposed workers and regions. I cannot verify the latest work from the materials here. I would want that evidence stated in the Committee's background material and not only asserted. It is also why I keep B032 as an alternative and not my preferred part. The credit line is the issue for me, not the science.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B014 first with Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. He objected to my opening trio of Woodford, Galí and Gertler because it credits the synthesis and application layer without the originators of staggered pricing and the policy rule. He agrees the Phillips-curve evidence is a real caveat that argues for careful citation wording.
responses.response: I accept the core of your objection. My opening trio chose the synthetic contributors because I was worried about credit allocation. It handles that worse than your trio, since it leaves out the two building blocks that define the framework. On attribution logic alone, Calvo, Taylor and Woodford is the more defensible cut within B014, and I no longer defend my opening trio. That does not move B014 to my preferred position. Eight names are credited, the choice between the theoretical originators and the estimation strand is one the Committee has not settled, and the evidence on the Phillips curve is mixed. I also remain unsure that the question of earlier macro prizes is as clear as you and Boppart say, though I accept your distinction between the methodological awards and a nominal-rigidity prize. I read your case as strong and mature, but one that depends on a choice of which strand to honour. For my purposes that is a more demanding attribution problem than the one in B010.

responses.point: Hassler, the chair, prefers B016 with Persson, Tabellini and Besley. He added Besley after Friberg's argument that state capacity is a distinct strand. He reads the overlap with the 2024 institutions prize as partial and grants that the cross-country constitutional evidence is partly observational.
responses.response: Your reply to me persuades me that the overlap with the 2024 prize is partial and not duplicative: that prize concerns long-run colonial-origin institutions, and B016 concerns how political rules and capacity shape fiscal and policy choices within existing states. My concern is the identification problem, which you share and which limits how strongly the empirical claims can be stated. I keep B016 as an alternative and not as my preferred part for that reason. I would also say that if the Committee chose B016, the choice between a two-person and a three-person award is a real one. Friberg himself calls Besley the most contestable part of his proposal, and you moved from two names to three on his argument. I regard Besley's state-capacity programme as a separable achievement, so the three-person version is defensible. But it makes the credit line less clean than B010's pair, which is where the comparison turns for me.

uncertainties: How the Committee should weigh the uncredited Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum lineage. I think wording the citation around the theoretical mechanism handles it, but members who prefer other candidates may not accept that.
Whether the quantitative debate on selection-based welfare gains is read as a debate about size, which the citation can avoid, or as a challenge to what the achievement is.
Whether Redding should be a third name. I treat his quantitative and spatial work as a separable later strand, and I cannot independently settle priority questions in the trade literature.

Whether B032 is more mature, and its evidence more checkable, than I have credited. This depends on re-examination evidence for shift-share inference and persistence that I cannot verify from the materials supplied.
Whether the Committee prefers to recognise trade through another strand, such as B003 or B041, which are outside the shortlist. I read B010 as the cleaner listed credit line but cannot rule that out.
Prior-prize facts (the 2008, 2022 and 2024 awards) rest on members' stated recollections and are not independently verified here.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent for B010 from the supplied profile. None of the credited names (Helpman, Melitz, Redding) is a co-author or documented close collaborator. My documented connections are the Uppsala and IFAU labour-economics network, including Bertil Holmlund, and an institutional overlap at Stockholm University with the IIES macro group, which is not a co-authorship. Holmlund is also listed as a frequent co-author of Committee member Hjalmarsson, a shared co-author and not a direct tie, and Hjalmarsson prefers B032. My own field, empirical labour economics, is closer to B032 than to B010, and I applied the common criteria and did not treat proximity as merit. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
